newsitem.title: KENYA: Closed Kenyan retail chain says free to reopen.
newsitem.headline: Closed Kenyan retail chain says free to reopen.

text.p: A Kenyan supermarket chain, closed on government orders over a "mad cow" scare, said on Wednesday the commerce ministry had abruptly changed tack and allowed its eight stores to reopen.
Nakumatt Holdings Ltd said the written reprieve came only two hours after Commerce and Industry Minister Kirugi M'Mukindia insisted the company's eight stores would remain closed.
Atul Shah, a Nakumatt director, told Reuters the stores would reopen his shops on Thursday morning.
"I want to carry on with my business. But this is a major contradiction between the minister and the ministry," he said.
There were no senior officials at the ministry on Wednesday evening to clarify matters.

Nakumatt stores were closed on September 19 when its trading licences were revoked on grounds it imported without proper approval 3.2 tonnes of corned beef from Britain, which has had outbreaks of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) or "mad cow" disease.
Earlier on Wednesday M'Mukindia told a Nairobi news conference the stores would stay shut.

"This beef is banned from importation to this country. If there is any indication of the worst form of capitalism, it is where a knowledgeable person, knowing the effects of the 'mad cow' disease, imports the same to be sold to people," he said.
Both Nakumatt and its supplier, British meat company John West, have stated the beef was from Brazil and packed there before being exported to Britain and re-exported to Kenya.

"Locally reared beef is used by our Brazilian supplier and this is not in any way associated with BSE," said the statement by John West, a subsidiary of the Unilever Group. "There is no reason why this consignment should be held."
Nakumatt took full-page advertisements in Kenyan newspapers on Tuesday to say mad cow disease was a pretext.
It said just before the closures it refused to pay a bribe of 50 million shillings ($893,000), demanded by an anonymous telephone caller, and linked its problems with anti-Asian sentiment.

M'Mukindia rejected as "traders' talk" the Nakumatt and John West statements: "On the basis of the evidence I have, this beef certainly comes from Britain. John West has made a statement, so has Nakumatt, they are all traders: traders talk. Kenya is not a dumping ground for poisons and this must be very clear."
He also rejected Nakumatt claims that it was targeted because it was owned by Kenyan Asians, and said Nakumatt should have reported to the police any blackmail attempts.
